title: 7th Semester B.Tech Mid-Semester Examination in Large Language Models
institution: Indian Institute of Information Technology Dharwad (IIIT Dharwad)
rules: No marks will be awarded if all parts of a question are not answered together.
Calculators and mathematical derivations must show intermediate steps.
Questions are evaluated according to the reconciled criterion rubric.

questions.text: Answer the following foundational LLM architectural and modeling questions (4 x 2 = 8 marks):

parts.question: What is the key limitation of traditional n-gram language models?
parts.model_answer: Traditional n-gram language models suffer from a fixed, limited context window governed by the n-1 Markov assumption and severe data sparsity / parameter explosion on unseen word combinations.

criteria.description: Identifies fixed/limited context window or n-1 Markov assumption limitation.
Identifies inability to capture long-range dependencies, data sparsity, or unseen n-gram explosion.

parts.question: Why is positional encoding required in transformers?
parts.model_answer: Because transformer self-attention processes all tokens in parallel without inherent sequential recurrence or convolutional inductive bias (it is permutation-invariant), positional encodings must be injected to preserve word order semantics.

criteria.description: Explains that parallel processing / self-attention is permutation-invariant with no inherent word order.
Explains the injection of sequence order/position semantics (sinusoidal formulation or word-order examples).

parts.question: What is the difference between encoder-only and decoder-only architectures?
parts.model_answer: Encoder-only architectures (e.g., BERT) employ bidirectional self-attention to construct contextual representations for classification/tagging, whereas decoder-only architectures (e.g., GPT) employ causal (autoregressive, left-to-right) masked attention for next-token generation.

criteria.description: Defines encoder-only architectures as bidirectional contextual representations (e.g. BERT).
Defines decoder-only architectures as causal/autoregressive left-to-right generators (e.g. GPT).

parts.question: What is masked attention and why is it used in GPT-like models?
parts.model_answer: Masked attention applies an upper-triangular mask (setting subsequent positions to -infinity before softmax) to prevent each token from attending to future tokens, ensuring the causal autoregressive property during next-token prediction.

criteria.description: Explains masking future tokens using an upper-triangular mask matrix M.
Explains preventing information leakage / maintaining causal autoregressive generation.

questions.text: Given Query Q = [1, 0], Keys K1 = [1, 1], K2 = [0, 1], and Values V1 = [2, 0], V2 = [0, 3], compute scaled dot-product attention components:

parts.question: Compute the dot-product attention scores for K1 and K2.

criteria.description: Correct computation of Q . K1 = 1.
Correct computation of Q . K2 = 0, yielding score vector [1, 0].

parts.question: Compute the softmax attention weights over the scores.

criteria.description: Correct formulation of softmax exponentials exp(1)/(exp(1)+exp(0)).
Correct numerical evaluation [0.731, 0.269] or rounded [0.73, 0.27].

parts.question: Compute the final context output vector.

criteria.description: Correct weighted linear combination of value vectors V1 and V2.
Correct final vector [1.462, 0.807] or rounded [1.46, 0.81].

questions.text: Given next-token probability distribution: Word A: 0.4, Word B: 0.3, Word C: 0.2, Word D: 0.1:

parts.question: Which word is chosen under greedy decoding?
parts.model_answer: Greedy decoding selects the word with the highest probability, which is Word A with probability 0.4.

criteria.description: Selects Word A due to highest probability 0.4.

parts.question: Which words are candidate selections under top-k decoding with k = 2?
parts.model_answer: Top-k decoding with k=2 filters to the top 2 words: Word A (0.4) and Word B (0.3). (Under temperature 0, Word A is chosen; candidates are Word A and Word B). Selecting Word C or D is an error.

criteria.description: Correctly selects Word A and Word B. Contradiction penalty if Word C/D selected.

parts.question: Why is layer normalization applied twice in each transformer block? (Dual-Valid Override: or explain top-p vs top-k)
parts.model_answer: Layer normalization is applied twice in each transformer block: once after the multi-head self-attention layer to stabilize attention activations, and once after the feed-forward network to stabilize intermediate representations and ensure consistent gradient flow across deep layers. (Alternatively, explaining top-p nucleus sampling vs top-k is also awarded full 1.0 mark due to solution key reconciliation).

criteria.description: Accurately explains dual LayerNorm (post-attention & post-FFN gradient stabilization) OR top-p vs top-k distinction.

questions.text: Compute the probability of sentence '<S> I like ML </S>' using a bigram language model with Add-1 (Laplace) smoothing given training corpus '<S> I like NLP </S>', '<S> I like AI </S>', and '<S> I love NLP </S>':

parts.question: Compute P(<S> I like ML </S>) with Add-1 smoothing.

criteria.description: Corpus boundary token augmentation (<S>, </S>) and bigram/unigram count extraction.
Application of Laplace Add-1 smoothing formula (C(w_{i-1}, w_i) + 1)/(C(w_{i-1}) + |V|) under valid |V| in {6, 7, 8}.
Chain rule product yielding valid fraction/decimal: 3/2420 (~0.00124), 0.000408 or 2/1050, or 3/12100. (Partial 1.0 mark if student only sets up isolated conditional probability).
